{{Short description|Theorem in functional analysis}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Grothendieck inequality''' states that there is a universal constant <math>K_G</math> with the following property. If ''M''<sub>''ij''</sub> is an ''n''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''n'' ([[real number|real]] or [[complex number|complex]]) [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] with
: <math>\Big| \sum_{i,j} M_{ij} s_i t_j \Big| \le 1</math>

for all (real or complex) numbers ''s''<sub>''i''</sub>, ''t''<sub>''j''</sub> of absolute value at most 1, then
: <math>\Big| \sum_{i,j} M_{ij} \langle S_i, T_j \rangle \Big| \le K_G</math>

for all [[vector (mathematics)|vectors]] ''S''<sub>''i''</sub>, ''T''<sub>''j''</sub> in the [[unit ball]] ''B''(''H'') of a (real or complex) [[Hilbert space]] ''H'', the constant <math>K_G</math> being independent of ''n''. For a fixed Hilbert space of dimension ''d'', the smallest constant that satisfies this property for all ''n''&nbsp;×&nbsp;''n'' matrices is called a '''Grothendieck constant''' and denoted <math>K_G(d)</math>. In fact, there are two Grothendieck constants, <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}(d)</math> and <math>K_G^{\mathbb C}(d)</math>, depending on whether one works with real or complex numbers, respectively.<ref>{{Citation | last = Pisier | first = Gilles | author-link = Gilles Pisier |date=April 2012 | title = Grothendieck's Theorem, Past and Present | journal = [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume = 49 | issue = 2 | pages = 237–323 | doi = 10.1090/S0273-0979-2011-01348-9 | arxiv = 1101.4195| s2cid = 119162963 }}.</ref><ref name="CCP">{{cite book | last = Oertel | first = Frank | title = Upper Bounds for Grothendieck Constants, Quantum Correlation Matrices and CCP Functions | year = 2024 | publisher = Springer | url = https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-031-57201-2 }}</ref>

The Grothendieck inequality and Grothendieck constants are named after [[Alexander Grothendieck]], who proved the existence of the constants in a paper published in 1953.<ref name="a"/>

== Motivation and the operator formulation ==
Let <math>A = (a_{ij})</math> be an <math>m \times n</math> matrix. Then <math>A</math> defines a linear operator between the normed spaces <math>(\mathbb R^n, \| \cdot \|_p)</math> and <math>(\mathbb R^m, \| \cdot \|_q)</math> for <math>1 \leq p, q \leq \infty</math>. The '''<math>(p \to q)</math>-norm''' of <math>A</math> is the quantity

<math>\| A \|_{p \to q} = \max_{x \in \mathbb R^n : \| x \|_p = 1} \| Ax \|_q.</math>

If <math>p = q</math>, we denote the norm by <math>\| A \|_p</math>.

One can consider the following question: For what value of <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> is <math>\| A \|_{p \to q}</math> maximized? Since <math>A</math> is linear, then it suffices to consider <math>p</math> such that <math>\{ x \in \mathbb R^n : \| x \|_p \leq 1 \}</math> contains as many points as possible, and also <math>q</math> such that <math>\| Ax \|_q</math> is as large as possible. By comparing <math>\| x \|_p</math> for <math>p = 1, 2, \ldots, \infty</math>, one sees that <math>\| A \|_{\infty \to 1} \geq \| A \|_{p \to q}</math> for all <math>1 \leq p, q \leq \infty</math>.

One way to compute <math>\| A \|_{\infty \to 1}</math> is by solving the following quadratic [[Integer programming|integer program]]:

<math>\begin{align} \max & \qquad \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} x_i y_j \\ \text{s.t.} & \qquad (x, y) \in \{ -1, 1 \}^{m + n} \end{align}</math>

To see this, note that <math>\sum_{i, j} A_{ij} x_i y_j = \sum_i (Ay)_i x_i</math>, and taking the maximum over <math>x \in \{ -1, 1 \}^m</math> gives <math>\| Ay \|_1</math>. Then taking the maximum over <math>y \in \{ -1, 1 \}^n</math> gives <math>\| A \|_{\infty \to 1}</math> by the convexity of <math>\{ x \in \mathbb R^m : \| x \|_\infty = 1 \}</math> and by the [[triangle inequality]]. This quadratic integer program can be relaxed to the following [[Semidefinite programming|semidefinite program]]:

<math>\begin{align} \max & \qquad \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} \langle x^{(i)}, y^{(j)} \rangle \\ \text{s.t.} & \qquad x^{(1)}, \ldots, x^{(m)}, y^{(1)}, \ldots, y^{(n)} \text{ are unit vectors in } (\mathbb R^d, \| \cdot \|_2) \end{align}</math>

It is known that exactly computing <math>\| A \|_{p \to q}</math> for <math>1 \leq q < p \leq \infty</math> is [[NP-hardness|NP-hard]], while exacting computing <math>\| A \|_p</math> is [[NP-hardness|NP-hard]] for <math>p \not \in \{ 1, 2, \infty \}</math>.

One can then ask the following natural question: How well does an optimal solution to the [[Semidefinite programming|semidefinite program]] approximate <math>\| A \|_{\infty \to 1}</math>? The Grothendieck inequality provides an answer to this question: There exists a fixed constant <math>C > 0</math> such that, for any <math>m, n \geq 1</math>, for any <math>m \times n</math> matrix <math>A</math>, and for any Hilbert space <math>H</math>,

<math>\max_{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)} \in H \text{ unit vectors}} \sum_{i, j} A_{ij} \left\langle x^{(i)}, y^{(j)} \right\rangle_H \leq C \| A \|_{\infty \to 1}.</math>

==Bounds on the constants==
The sequences <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}(d)</math> and <math>K_G^{\mathbb C}(d)</math> are easily seen to be increasing, and Grothendieck's result states that they are [[bounded sequence|bounded]],<ref name="a">{{Citation | last1=Grothendieck | first1=Alexander | author1-link=Alexander Grothendieck | title=Résumé de la théorie métrique des produits tensoriels topologiques | mr=0094682  | year=1953 | journal=Bol. Soc. Mat. Sao Paulo | volume=8 | pages=1–79}}.</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=Blei | first1=Ron C. | title=An elementary proof of the Grothendieck inequality | jstor=2046119 | mr=883401  | year=1987 | journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] | issn=0002-9939 | volume=100 | issue=1 | pages=58–60 | doi=10.2307/2046119 | publisher=American Mathematical Society| doi-access=free }}.</ref> so they have [[limit of a sequence|limits]].

Grothendieck proved that <math>1.57 \approx \frac{\pi}{2} \leq K_G^{\mathbb R} \leq \operatorname{sinh}\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 2.3,</math> where <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}</math> is defined to be <math>\sup_d K_G^{\mathbb R}(d)</math>.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Finch | first1=Steven R. | author-link=Steven R. Finch | title=Mathematical constants | publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] | isbn=978-0-521-81805-6 | year=2003 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/mathematicalcons0000finc }}.</ref>

{{harvtxt|Krivine|1979}}<ref name="krivine">{{Citation | last1=Krivine | first1=J.-L. | title=Constantes de Grothendieck et fonctions de type positif sur les sphères | doi=10.1016/0001-8708(79)90017-3 | mr=521464  | year=1979 | journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]] | issn=0001-8708 | volume=31 | issue=1 | pages=16–30| doi-access=free }}.</ref> improved the upper bound by proving that <math>K_G^{\mathbb R} \le \frac{\pi}{2 \ln(1 + \sqrt{2})} \approx 1.78221398</math>, conjecturing that it is tight.<ref name="CCP"/> However, this conjecture was disproved by {{harvtxt|Braverman|Makarychev|Makarychev|Naor|2011}}.<ref name="braverman">{{citation
 | last1 = Braverman | first1 = Mark
 | last2 = Makarychev | first2 = Konstantin
 | last3 = Makarychev | first3 = Yury
 | last4 = Naor | first4 = Assaf
 | arxiv = 1103.6161
 | contribution = The Grothendieck Constant is Strictly Smaller than Krivine's Bound
 | doi = 10.1109/FOCS.2011.77
 | pages = 453–462
 | title = [[Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science|52nd Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)]]
 | year = 2011| isbn = 978-0-7695-4571-4
 | s2cid = 7803437
 }}.</ref>  They did not provide an explicit upper bound, but it seems their argument showed that <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}<\frac{\pi}{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})}-10^{-500} </math>.

The best numerical lower bound for <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}</math> was <math>\approx 1.67696 </math> by {{harvtxt|Davie|1984}}.<ref name="davie1984"/> This was shown not to be optimal by {{harvtxt|Heilman|2026a}}<ref name ="heilmana">{{cite arxiv |last=Heilman |first=Steven |title=A Lower Bound for Grothendieck's Constant |date=2026 |eprint=2603.22616 |class=math.FA}}</ref> and {{harvtxt|Jones|Malavolta|2026}}.<ref name ="jones">{{cite arxiv |last1=Jones |first1=Chris |last2=Malavolta |first2=Giulio |title=The Grothendieck Constant is Strictly Larger than Davie-Reeds' Bound |date=2026 |eprint=2603.30039 |class=math.FA}}</ref>

The best numerical upper bound for <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}</math> is <math>\frac{\pi}{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})}-6.039\cdot 10^{-5}\approx 1.7821536 </math> by {{harvtxt|Li|Saha|Xue|Chaudhuri|Klivans|Kothari|Meka|2026}},<ref name="li">{{cite arxiv |last1=Li |first1=Alan| last2=Saha| first2=Rahul| last3=Xue| first3=Anton| last4=Chaudhuri| first4=Swarat| last5=Klivans| first5=Adam| last6=Kothari| first6=Pravesh| last7=Meka| first7=Raghu |title=The Grothendieck Constant is Less Than \frac{\pi}{2 \log (1+ \sqrt{2})} - 10^{-5} |date=2026 |eprint=2606.03991 |class=cs.DS}}</ref> with concurrent improvement of <math>\frac{\pi}{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})}-10^{-5}</math> in {{harvtxt|Heilman|2026b}}.<ref name="heilmanb">{{cite arxiv |last=Heilman |first=Steven |title=An Upper Bound on Grothendieck's Constant |date=2026 |eprint=2606.00247 |class=math.FA}}</ref>

==Grothendieck constant of order ''d''==

[[Boris Tsirelson]] showed that the Grothendieck constants <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}(d)</math> play an essential role in the problem of [[quantum nonlocality]]: the [[Tsirelson bound]] of any full correlation bipartite [[Bell inequality]] for a quantum system of dimension ''d'' is upperbounded by <math>K_G^{\mathbb R}(2d^2)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Boris Tsirelson |title=Quantum analogues of the Bell inequalities. The case of two spatially separated domains |journal=Journal of Soviet Mathematics |date=1987 |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=557–570 |doi=10.1007/BF01663472 |s2cid=119363229 |url=http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~tsirel/download/qbell87.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=Acín | first1=Antonio | last2=Gisin | first2=Nicolas | last3=Toner | first3=Benjamin  | title=Grothendieck's constant and local models for noisy entangled quantum states | journal=[[Physical Review A]] | year=2006| volume=73 | issue=6 | article-number=062105 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.73.062105 | arxiv=quant-ph/0606138 | bibcode=2006PhRvA..73f2105A | s2cid=2588399 }}.</ref>

== Applications ==

=== Cut norm estimation ===
Given an <math>m \times n</math> real matrix <math>A = (a_{ij})</math>, the '''cut norm''' of <math>A</math> is defined by

: <math>\| A \|_\square = \max_{S \subset [m],  T \subset [n]}  \left| \sum_{i \in S, j \in T} a_{ij} \right|.</math>

The notion of cut norm is essential in designing efficient approximation algorithms for dense graphs and matrices. More generally, the definition of cut norm can be generalized for symmetric [[Measurable function|measurable]] functions <math>W : [0, 1]^2 \to \mathbb R </math> so that the '''cut norm''' of <math>W </math> is defined by

: <math>\| W \|_\square = \sup_{S, T \subset [0, 1]} \left| \int_{S \times T} W \right|. </math>

This generalized definition of cut norm is crucial in the study of the space of [[graphon]]s, and the two definitions of cut norm can be linked via the [[adjacency matrix]] of a [[Graph theory|graph]].

An application of the Grothendieck inequality is to give an efficient algorithm for approximating the cut norm of a given real matrix <math>A</math>; specifically, given an <math>m \times n</math> real matrix, one can find a number <math>\alpha</math> such that

<math>\| A \|_\square \leq \alpha \leq C \| A \|_\square,</math>

where <math>C</math> is an absolute constant.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Alon|first1=Noga|last2=Naor|first2=Assaf|date=January 2006|title=Approximating the Cut-Norm via Grothendieck's Inequality|url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0097539704441629|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing|language=en|volume=35|issue=4|pages=787–803|doi=10.1137/S0097539704441629|issn=0097-5397|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This approximation algorithm uses [[semidefinite programming]].

We give a sketch of this approximation algorithm. Let <math>B = (b_{ij})</math> be <math>(m + 1) \times (n + 1)</math> matrix defined by

<math>\begin{pmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & \ldots & a_{1n} & -\sum_{k = 1}^n a_{1k} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} & \ldots & a_{2n} & -\sum_{k = 1}^n a_{2k} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\ a_{m1} & a_{m2} & \ldots & a_{mn} & -\sum_{k = 1}^n a_{mk} \\ -\sum_{\ell = 1}^m a_{\ell 1} & -\sum_{\ell = 1}^m a_{\ell 2} & \ldots & -\sum_{\ell = 1}^m a_{\ell n} & \sum_{k = 1}^n \sum_{\ell = 1}^m a_{\ell k} \end{pmatrix}.</math>

One can verify that <math>\| A \|_\square = \| B \|_\square</math> by observing, if <math>S \in [m + 1], T \in [n + 1]</math> form a maximizer for the cut norm of <math>B</math>, then

<math>S^* = \begin{cases} S, & \text{if } m + 1 \not \in S, \\ {[m]} \setminus S, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \qquad
T^* = \begin{cases} T, & \text{if } n + 1 \not \in T, \\ {[n]} \setminus S, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \qquad</math>

form a maximizer for the cut norm of <math>A</math>. Next, one can verify that <math>\| B \|_\square = \| B \|_{\infty \to 1}/4</math>, where

<math>\| B \|_{\infty \to 1} = \max \left\{ \sum_{i = 1}^{m + 1} \sum_{j = 1}^{n + 1} b_{ij} \varepsilon_i \delta_j : \varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_{m + 1} \in \{ -1, 1 \}, \delta_1, \ldots, \delta_{n + 1} \in \{ -1, 1 \} \right\}.</math><ref name=":0" />

Although not important in this proof, <math>\| B \|_{\infty \to 1}</math> can be interpreted to be the norm of <math>B</math> when viewed as a linear operator from <math>\ell_\infty^m</math> to <math>\ell_1^m</math>.

Now it suffices to design an efficient algorithm for approximating <math>\| A \|_{\infty \to 1}</math>. We consider the following [[Semidefinite programming|semidefinite program]]:

<math>\text{SDP}(A) = \max \left\{ \sum_{i = 1}^m \sum_{j = 1}^n a_{ij} \left\langle x_i, y_j \right\rangle : x_1, \ldots, x_m, y_1, \ldots, y_n \in S^{n + m - 1} \right\}.</math>

Then <math>\text{SDP}(A) \geq \| A \|_{\infty \to 1}</math>. The Grothedieck inequality implies that <math>\text{SDP}(A) \leq K_G^{\mathbb R} \| A \|_{\infty \to 1}</math>. Many algorithms (such as [[interior-point method]]s, first-order methods, the bundle method, the [[augmented Lagrangian method]]) are known to output the value of a semidefinite program up to an additive error <math>\varepsilon</math> in time that is polynomial in the program description size and <math>\log (1/\varepsilon)</math>.<ref>{{Cite book|last=P.|first=Boyd, Stephen|title=Convex optimization|date=2011|publisher=Cambridge Univ. Pr|isbn=978-0-521-83378-3|oclc=767754283}}</ref> Therefore, one can output <math>\alpha = \text{SDP}(B)</math> which satisfies

<math>\| A \|_\square \leq \alpha \leq C \| A \|_\square \qquad \text{with} \qquad C = K_G^{\mathbb R}. </math>

=== Szemerédi's regularity lemma ===
[[Szemerédi regularity lemma|Szemerédi's regularity lemma]] is a useful tool in graph theory, asserting (informally) that any graph can be partitioned into a controlled number of pieces that interact with each other in a [[Pseudorandom graph|pseudorandom]] way. Another application of the Grothendieck inequality is to produce a partition of the vertex set that satisfies the conclusion of [[Szemerédi regularity lemma|Szemerédi's regularity lemma]], via the cut norm estimation algorithm, in time that is polynomial in the upper bound of Szemerédi's regular partition size but independent of the number of vertices in the graph.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Khot|first1=Subhash|last2=Naor|first2=Assaf|date=2012-04-25|title=Grothendieck-Type Inequalities in Combinatorial Optimization|journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics|volume=65|issue=7|pages=992–1035|doi=10.1002/cpa.21398|arxiv=1108.2464 |s2cid=3175317 |issn=0010-3640}}</ref>

It turns out that the main "bottleneck" of constructing a Szemeredi's regular partition in polynomial time is to determine in polynomial time whether or not a given pair <math>(X, Y)</math> is close to being '''<math>\varepsilon</math>-regular''', meaning that for all <math>S \subset X, T \subset Y</math> with <math>|S| \geq \varepsilon |X|, |T| \geq \varepsilon |Y|</math>, we have

<math>\left| \frac{e(S, T)}{|S||T|} - \frac{e(X, Y)}{|X||Y|} \right| \leq \varepsilon,</math>

where <math>e(X', Y') = |\{ (u, v) \in X' \times Y' : uv \in E \}|</math> for all <math>X', Y' \subset V</math> and <math>V, E</math> are the vertex and edge sets of the graph, respectively. To that end, we construct an <math>n \times n</math> matrix <math>A = (a_{xy})_{(x, y) \in X \times Y}</math>, where <math>n = |V|</math>, defined by

<math>a_{xy} = \begin{cases} 1 - \frac{e(X, Y)}{|X||Y|}, & \text{if } xy \in E, \\ -\frac{e(X, Y)}{|X||Y|}, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}</math>

Then for all <math>S \subset X, T \subset Y</math>,

<math>\left| \sum_{x \in S, y \in T} a_{xy} \right| = |S||T| \left| \frac{e(S, T)}{|S||T|} - \frac{e(X, Y)}{|X||Y|} \right|.</math>

Hence, if <math>(X, Y)</math> is not <math>\varepsilon</math>-regular, then <math>\| A \|_\square \geq \varepsilon^3 n^2</math>. It follows that using the cut norm approximation algorithm together with the rounding technique, one can find in polynomial time <math>S \subset X, T \subset Y</math> such that

<math>\min\left\{ n|S|, n|T|, n^2 \left| \frac{e(S, T)}{|S||T|} - \frac{e(X, Y)}{|X||Y|} \right| \right\} \geq \left|\sum_{x \in S, y \in T} a_{xy}\right| \geq \frac{1}{K_G^{\mathbb R}} \varepsilon^3 n^2 \geq \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon^3 n^2.</math>

Then the algorithm for producing a Szemerédi's regular partition follows from the constructive argument of Alon et al.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Alon|first=N.|title=Proceedings., 33rd Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science |chapter=The algorithmic aspects of the regularity lemma |date=1992|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/sfcs.1992.267804|pages=473–481 |publisher=IEEE|doi=10.1109/sfcs.1992.267804|isbn=0-8186-2900-2 |s2cid=2222009 }}</ref>

== Variants of the Grothendieck inequality ==

=== Grothendieck inequality of a graph ===
The '''Grothendieck inequality of a graph''' states that for each <math>n \in \mathbb N</math> and for each graph <math>G = (\{ 1, \ldots, n \}, E)</math> without self loops, there exists a universal constant <math>K > 0</math> such that every <math>n \times n</math> matrix <math>A = (a_{ij})</math> satisfies that

<math>\max_{x_1, \ldots, x_n \in S^{n - 1}} \sum_{ij \in E} a_{ij} \left\langle x_i, x_j \right\rangle \leq K \max_{\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n \in \{ -1, 1 \}} \sum_{ij \in E} a_{ij} \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j.</math><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Alon|first1=Noga|last2=Makarychev|first2=Konstantin|last3=Makarychev|first3=Yury|last4=Naor|first4=Assaf|date=2006-03-01|title=Quadratic forms on graphs|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|language=en|volume=163|issue=3|pages=499–522|doi=10.1007/s00222-005-0465-9|issn=1432-1297}}</ref>

The '''Grothendieck constant of a graph''' <math>G</math>, denoted <math>K(G)</math>, is defined to be the smallest constant <math>K</math> that satisfies the above property.

The Grothendieck inequality of a graph is an extension of the Grothendieck inequality because the former inequality is the special case of the latter inequality when <math>G</math> is a [[bipartite graph]] with two copies of <math>\{ 1, \ldots, n \}</math> as its bipartition classes. Thus,

<math>K_G = \sup_{n \in \mathbb N} \{ K(G) : G \text{ is an } n \text{-vertex bipartite graph} \}.</math>

For <math>G = K_n</math>, the <math>n</math>-vertex [[complete graph]], the Grothendieck inequality of <math>G</math> becomes

<math>\max_{x_1, \ldots, x_n \in S^{n - 1}} \sum_{i, j \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}, i \neq j} a_{ij} \left\langle x_i, x_j \right\rangle \leq K(K_n) \max_{\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n \in \{ -1, 1 \}} \sum_{i, j \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}, i \neq j} a_{ij} \varepsilon_i \varepsilon_j.</math>

It turns out that <math>K(K_n) \asymp \log n</math>. On one hand, we have <math>K(K_n) \lesssim \log n</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nemirovski|first1=A.|last2=Roos|first2=C.|last3=Terlaky|first3=T.|date=1999-12-01|title=On maximization of quadratic form over intersection of ellipsoids with common center|journal=Mathematical Programming|language=en|volume=86|issue=3|pages=463–473|doi=10.1007/s101070050100|s2cid=2988923 |issn=1436-4646}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Megretski|first=Alexandre|title=Systems, Approximation, Singular Integral Operators, and Related Topics |chapter=Relaxations of Quadratic Programs in Operator Theory and System Analysis |date=2001|editor-last=Borichev|editor-first=Alexander A.|editor2-last=Nikolski|editor2-first=Nikolai K.|chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007%2F978-3-0348-8362-7_15|series=Operator Theory: Advances and Applications|language=en|location=Basel|publisher=Birkhäuser|pages=365–392|doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-8362-7_15|isbn=978-3-0348-8362-7}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Charikar|first1=M.|last2=Wirth|first2=A.|title=45th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science |chapter=Maximizing Quadratic Programs: Extending Grothendieck's Inequality |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/focs.2004.39|year=2004 |pages=54–60 |publisher=IEEE|doi=10.1109/focs.2004.39|isbn=0-7695-2228-9 |s2cid=7036076 }}</ref> Indeed, the following inequality is true for any <math>n \times n</math> matrix <math>A = (a_{ij})</math>, which implies that <math>K(K_n) \lesssim \log n</math> by the [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality|Cauchy-Schwarz inequality]]:<ref name=":1" />

<math>\max_{x_1, \ldots, x_n \in S^{n - 1}} \sum_{i, j \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}, i \neq j} a_{ij} \left\langle x_i, x_j \right\rangle \leq \log\left(\frac{\sum_{i \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}} \sum_{j \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \} \setminus \{ i \}} |a_{ij}|}{\sqrt{\sum_{i \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}} \sum_{j \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \} \setminus \{ i \}} a_{ij}^2}}\right) \max_{\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n \in \{ -1, 1 \}} \sum_{i, j \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}, i \neq j} a_{ij} \varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_n.</math>

On the other hand, the matching lower bound <math>K(K_n) \gtrsim \log n</math> is due to [[Noga Alon|Alon]], Makarychev, Makarychev and [[Assaf Naor|Naor]] in 2006.<ref name=":1" />

The Grothendieck inequality <math>K(G)</math> of a graph <math>G</math> depends upon the structure of <math>G</math>. It is known that

<math>\log \omega \lesssim K(G) \lesssim \log \vartheta,</math><ref name=":1" />

and

<math>K(G) \leq \frac{\pi}{2\log\left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{(\vartheta - 1)^2 + 1}}{\vartheta - 1}\right)},</math><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Briet|first1=Jop|last2=de Oliveira Filho|first2=Fernando Mario|last3=Vallentin|first3=Frank|date=2014|title=Grothendieck Inequalities for Semidefinite Programs with Rank Constraint|url=http://www.theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v010a004|journal=Theory of Computing|language=en|volume=10|issue=1|pages=77–105|doi=10.4086/toc.2014.v010a004|s2cid=1004947 |issn=1557-2862|doi-access=free|arxiv=1011.1754}}</ref>

where <math>\omega</math> is the [[Clique (graph theory)|clique number]] of <math>G</math>, i.e., the largest <math>k \in \{ 2, \ldots, n \}</math> such that there exists <math>S \subset \{ 1, \ldots, n \}</math> with <math>|S| = k</math> such that <math>ij \in E</math> for all distinct <math>i, j \in S</math>, and

<math>\vartheta = \min \left\{ \max_{i \in \{ 1, \ldots, n \}} \frac{1}{\langle x_i, y \rangle} : x_1, \ldots, x_n, y \in S^n, \left\langle x_i, x_j \right\rangle = 0 \;\forall ij \in E \right\}.</math>

The parameter <math>\vartheta</math> is known as the [[Lovász theta function]] of the complement of <math>G</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lovasz|first=L.|date=January 1979|title=On the Shannon capacity of a graph|journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory|language=en|volume=25|issue=1|pages=1–7|doi=10.1109/TIT.1979.1055985|issn=0018-9448}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Karger|first1=David|last2=Motwani|first2=Rajeev|last3=Sudan|first3=Madhu|date=1998-03-01|title=Approximate graph coloring by semidefinite programming|journal=Journal of the ACM|volume=45|issue=2|pages=246–265|doi=10.1145/274787.274791|issn=0004-5411}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

=== L^p Grothendieck inequality ===
In the application of the Grothendieck inequality for approximating the cut norm, we have seen that the Grothendieck inequality answers the following question: How well does an optimal solution to the semidefinite program <math>\text{SDP}(A)</math> approximate <math>\| A \|_{\infty \to 1}</math>, which can be viewed as an optimization problem over the unit cube? More generally, we can ask similar questions over convex bodies other than the unit cube.

For instance, the following inequality is due to Naor and Schechtman and independently due to Guruswami et al:<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Guruswami|first1=Venkatesan|last2=Raghavendra|first2=Prasad|last3=Saket|first3=Rishi|last4=Wu|first4=Yi|date=2012-01-17|title=Bypassing UGC from some Optimal Geometric Inapproximability Results|journal=Proceedings of the Twenty-Third Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms|pages=699–717 |location=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|doi=10.1137/1.9781611973099.58|isbn=978-1-61197-210-8 }}</ref> For every <math>n \times n</math> matrix <math>A = (a_{ij})</math> and every <math>p \geq 2</math>,

<math>\max_{x_1, \ldots, x_n \in \mathbb R^n, \sum_{k = 1}^n \| x_k \|_2^p \leq 1} \sum_{i = 1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n a_{ij} \left\langle x_i, x_j \right\rangle \leq \gamma_p^2 \max_{t_1, \ldots, t_n \in \mathbb R, \sum_{k = 1}^n | t_k |^p \leq 1} \sum_{i = 1}^n \sum_{j = 1}^n a_{ij} t_i t_j,</math>

where

<math>\gamma_p = \sqrt{2} \left(\frac{\Gamma((p + 1)/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{1/p}.</math>

The constant <math>\gamma_p^2</math> is sharp in the inequality. [[Stirling's approximation|Stirling's formula]] implies that <math>\gamma_p^2 = p/e + O(1)</math> as <math>p \to \infty</math>.
